opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think coding agents are one of the most exciting places in agentic AI right now, for a few reasons.

First, code is an unusually good domain for agents because you can often verify whether the work is right. You can run the code, run unit tests, look at error messages, and iterate. That tight feedback loop is exactly what agentic workflows need. When I talk about agentic design patterns like reflection, tool use, planning, and multi-agent collaboration, coding is where all of those come together really naturally. An agent writes some code, executes it, sees it fail, reflects on why, and tries again. That loop works remarkably well.

Second, the economic value is very concrete. Software engineering is a large part of the economy, and we're already seeing developers get meaningful productivity gains, not just from autocomplete, but from agents that can take a higher-level task, explore a codebase, make changes across multiple files, and propose a pull request. The shift from "AI suggests the next line" to "AI takes on a whole task" is a big one.

Third, and this is the part I find most interesting, coding agents are lowering the barrier to building software. I've been encouraging everyone, not just engineers, to learn to code, and I think that advice is more relevant now, not less. When you can tell a computer precisely what you want, with the help of an AI coding assistant, you become dramatically more productive. Product managers, marketers, researchers, people who couldn't build a prototype before can now build one in an afternoon. That changes how teams work. One thing I've noticed is that the bottleneck is shifting from writing code to deciding what to build, so product management and clear specification are becoming more important.

And finally, coding agents are a great testbed for the rest of agentic AI. The lessons we learn here, about evals, about breaking work into steps, about when to keep a human in the loop, transfer to agents in other domains. So I think a lot of the frontier of agentic AI is being worked out in coding first.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think coding agents are the first place where agentic AI is really, clearly working at scale, and it's worth asking why that is. Code has a property that most other domains don't have: you can run it. The agent writes something, executes it, sees the error, and tries again. That tight feedback loop is exactly what agentic workflows need. When I talk about reflection, tool use, planning, multi-agent collaboration as the building blocks of agentic systems, coding is the domain where all four come together naturally, and the environment itself tells you whether you got it right.

The second thing is that the training data is unusually good. There's an enormous amount of code online, a lot of it paired with tests, issues, and discussion about why something was done a certain way. So the models have a strong prior not just about syntax, but about how software engineers reason.

What I find most exciting, though, is what this does for the rest of AI. Building applications has always been bottlenecked by how fast you can write and iterate on code. Now I see teams, including students who have never shipped software before, prototyping in an afternoon what used to take weeks. It changes what's economical to try. You can build twenty small experiments and throw away nineteen of them, and that's a very different way to do product development.

I'd add one caution. People hear "coding agent" and assume software engineering is going away. I don't think that's the picture. The people who understand how to decompose a problem, specify what they want, and evaluate whether the output is correct are becoming more valuable, not less. I actually tell people now that everyone should learn to code, precisely because the tooling has made it so much more leveraged. The agent handles the typing. You still need to know what you're asking for.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is exciting because an agent can take an action and get feedback. It can write a piece of code, run it, see an error, and then try to fix it. That ability to close the loop makes coding a particularly promising setting for agentic AI.

And the opportunity goes beyond helping software engineers type faster. If we can lower the cost of building software, we can build many more applications—especially applications that serve a small group of people or solve a very specific problem that previously wasn’t worth the engineering effort.

There are still challenges. Passing a test doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve built what the user wanted. But coding brings together planning, tool use, and iteration in a setting where you can often measure progress. That makes it a useful place to develop agents and learn what actually works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is exciting because an agent can actually check its own work. It can write some code, run it, look at the error message, revise it, and run it again. That feedback loop gives it a way to make progress beyond what it can get right in a single response.

And coding brings together a lot of the capabilities we want in agents: planning, using tools, reasoning over a large amount of context, and recovering when something goes wrong. The challenge is getting all of those pieces to work reliably over a longer task.

The other thing is that code is a way to take action. If an agent can write a small program to analyze some data or automate a workflow, its usefulness extends well beyond helping software engineers. So I see coding agents both as a valuable application and as a place to develop capabilities that will make many other kinds of agents more useful.
